sentences.text: You've tried to change before.
You started strong.
And by week two, life got in the way.
That's not a willpower problem.
Researchers found that about four in ten things we do each day, we do out of habit, often while thinking about something else.
So the secret isn't trying harder.
It's making the good thing automatic.
And the best habit books agree on how.
One.
Start so small you can't say no.
Two minutes.
One page.
One slow breath.
Small enough that even a bad day can't stop you.
Two.
Tie it to something you already do.
After I brush my teeth, I floss one tooth.
The old habit becomes the reminder.
Three.
Plan for the hard day before it comes.
If I'm tired, I'll do just one minute.
People who decide their backup ahead of time are more likely to follow through.
Four.
Every time you do it, it's a little proof of who you're becoming.
So stop for a second, and feel good about it.
That feeling helps a habit stick.
And when you miss a day, and you will, be kind to yourself.
One missed day changes almost nothing.
Just don't miss two.
One study found a new habit took about sixty-six days, on average, to feel automatic.
For some people much less, for others much more.
It's not a sprint.
It's a few minutes a day, growing a little at a time.
That's how Tadapop helps.
You pick what matters to you.
We build a tiny plan around your day, grow it a little each week, ask how it's going, and adjust when life gets hard.
Pick one thing.
Start small.
Start today.
